prompt: What is a cold start?
hint: What has to exist before a handler can be called?

choices.text: Lambda's own service waking up after a quiet period
choices.why: The service is always up. What is missing is an environment for this function.

choices.text: A new environment being built before the handler gets the request
choices.why: Right. Placing it, starting the runtime and importing your module are the init phase.

choices.text: The handler running slowly the first time because Python compiles it
choices.why: Compiling to bytecode is a small part. The init phase is mostly the runtime and your imports.

choices.text: The caller's network opening a connection to AWS
choices.why: That happens on warm requests too. A cold start is on the function's side.

prompt: Put what happens to a cold request in order.
hint: Init first, then invoke.
items: Lambda places an environment and fetches the code
The runtime imports your module, running its top level
The runtime calls the handler with the event
The handler's return value goes back to the caller
trap: Your top-level code runs before the handler is called, not on its first line.

prompt: Which of these run in the init phase? Choose all that apply.
hint: The init phase is the import of the module.

choices.text: An import boto3 at the top of the file
choices.why: Right. Top-level imports run when the module is imported.

choices.text: A client built at the top of the file
choices.why: Right. Anything at module level runs at init.

choices.text: A client built inside the handler
choices.why: That runs in the invoke phase, on every call.

choices.text: The handler's return statement
choices.why: The handler runs in the invoke phase.

choices.text: A configuration file read at module level
choices.why: Right. It is read once, when the module is imported.

prompt: In the emulator, a module that builds a client shows Init Duration: 0.06 ms and Duration: 306.68 ms on its first REPORT. Where is the length of its init phase?
hint: The emulator gets one field wrong.

choices.text: In Init Duration, as on AWS: the client cost almost nothing
choices.why: On AWS that field is right; in the emulator it prints a few milliseconds at most, whatever the module does.

choices.text: In Billed Duration minus Duration
choices.why: That difference is the rounding up to the next millisecond.

choices.text: In the durationMs of the INIT REPORT line
choices.why: Right. The emulator measures the init phase there, and folds it into the first Duration.

choices.text: In the time curl printed for the second call
choices.why: The second call is warm; it has no init phase at all.

prompt: On AWS, the REPORT line of a cold request gives the length of its init phase in the field Init ___.
hint: The field the emulator gets wrong.

prompt: On the laptop, the bare handler's init phase took 48 ms and the eager one's, which imports boto3 and builds a client, 301 ms. How many milliseconds of the eager init are the import and the client?
hint: The runtime's part is the same in both.

prompt: Moving the client from the top of the file into the handler gave a short init phase. What did it do to the function?
hint: Look at the first call and then at the warm ones.

choices.text: Made it faster overall, because init is what a cold start costs
choices.why: The first call paid the same import instead, and the warm calls got slower.

choices.text: The cold request stayed as slow, and each warm one rebuilds the client
choices.why: Right. About 8 ms per warm call against under 1 ms, on nearly every request.

choices.text: It slowed the first call alone, and left the warm calls as they were
choices.why: Python keeps the module, so the import is free, but the client is built on every call.

choices.text: It skipped the import on warm calls, so it wins under traffic
choices.why: Skipping the import is right; the client is still rebuilt, which is the part that costs.

prompt: A 1 GB function in sa-east-1 is billed 8 ms per warm request with the client built in the handler, and 1 ms with it built at the top of the file. At 0.0000166667 USD per GB-second, what do 10,000,000 warm requests a month cost extra the first way, in USD to the cent?
hint: 7 ms of difference, times the requests, times 1 GB, times the price.

prompt: When is building something inside the handler, on first use, the right choice?
hint: Think of a dependency not every request needs.

choices.text: For any client, so that the init phase stays short
choices.why: That moves the cost to the first call and repeats it on warm calls unless it is kept.

choices.text: For a rarely needed dependency, kept in a global
choices.why: Right. Requests that never need it never pay for it, and the rest pay once per environment.

choices.text: When the function has provisioned concurrency
choices.why: Provisioned environments run the init phase in advance, so moving work out of it gains nothing.

choices.text: When the function is called rarely, so most requests are cold
choices.why: A cold request pays the work either way; where it runs makes no difference to it.

prompt: Match each line of the emulator's log to what it marks.
hint: Init lines, invoke lines, and the one field that misleads.

pairs.right: The container starting the runtime's bootstrap
The init phase, as the emulator measures it
The handler being called for one request
On AWS, the init phase of a cold request

prompt: A function's init builds three SDK clients and parses a large schema. It runs at 128 MB on Lambda, and somebody raises it to 1,024 MB. What happens to its cold start?
hint: What else comes with memory on Lambda?

choices.text: Nothing: memory decides how much the function can hold, not how fast it runs
choices.why: On Lambda, CPU is given in proportion to memory, so a CPU-bound init speeds up.

choices.text: It gets longer, because more memory has to be prepared
choices.why: Preparing memory is not what the init phase is made of; computation is.

choices.text: The warm requests speed up while the init runs on a fixed CPU
choices.why: The init phase runs on the same CPU share as the handler.

choices.text: It gets shorter, because the CPU share grows with memory
choices.why: Right. The emulator showed the same with Docker's --cpus: 343 ms on one CPU, 1337 on a quarter.

prompt: python3 -X importtime prints boto3 with 221273 in its middle column. What is that number?
hint: Self, cumulative, module.

choices.text: Microseconds for boto3 and everything it imported in turn
choices.why: Right. The cumulative time, about 221 ms, mostly botocore.

choices.text: Microseconds for boto3's own code, its imports not counted
choices.why: That is the first column, the module's own time.

choices.text: Microseconds since the interpreter started
choices.why: The column is per module, not a clock.

choices.text: The bytes of memory boto3 took when it was imported
choices.why: importtime measures time only; memory needs another tool.

prompt: A function runs 0.6 s per request at 512 MB in sa-east-1, at 0.0000166667 USD per GB-second. What does the duration of 1,000,000 requests cost, in USD to the cent?
hint: 0.5 GB × 0.6 s per request.

prompt: Which of these shorten a cold start without adding to the bill? Choose all that apply.
hint: Some move the work, some remove it, some are paid.

choices.text: Removing an import the function never uses
choices.why: Right. Less work in the init phase, for nothing.

choices.text: Building the clients at module level instead of in the handler
choices.why: That speeds up the warm requests; the cold one pays the same work either way.

choices.text: Keeping the package small, so there is less to fetch
choices.why: Right. On AWS the code is fetched in the init phase.

choices.text: Provisioned concurrency for the busy hours
choices.why: It removes the cold start, and it is billed for every second it is configured.

choices.text: A ping every five minutes
choices.why: It keeps one environment warm, adds invocations, and leaves a burst cold.

prompt: A team packages its own boto3 instead of relying on the runtime's copy. What do they gain, and what does it cost?
hint: Who updates the runtime's copy, and when?

choices.text: A faster import, because a packaged copy is precompiled
choices.why: The packaged copy is the same Python; the import costs the same.

choices.text: A version they control, for about 27 MB more to fetch on each cold start
choices.why: Right. AWS updates the runtime's copy on its own schedule; a pinned copy does not move.

choices.text: A smaller package, because the runtime's copy is then removed
choices.why: The runtime's copy stays in the runtime; theirs is added to the package.

choices.text: Nothing, because Lambda ignores a boto3 inside the package
choices.why: The package comes first on the path, so its boto3 is the one imported.

prompt: What does moving a Python function from x86 to Arm do, according to the sheet and AWS's documentation?
hint: Compare the two duration lines, and recall what AWS promises.

choices.text: A faster cold start, which is the reason it costs less
choices.why: AWS does not promise a faster cold start on Arm; the price is the documented difference.

choices.text: The same price per GB-second, with more memory per gigabyte
choices.why: A gigabyte is a gigabyte; the price per GB-second is what differs.

choices.text: A fifth off each GB-second, and no promised speed-up
choices.why: Right. 0.0000133334 against 0.0000166667, and a cold start you would have to measure.

choices.text: Cheaper requests, at the same price per GB-second
choices.why: The request price is the same; the duration price is what Arm lowers.

prompt: What does SnapStart do?
hint: It moves the init phase to a different moment.

choices.text: Keeps environments initialised in advance and bills them by the second
choices.why: That is provisioned concurrency.

choices.text: Runs init once at publish and restores it on each cold start
choices.why: Right. The interpreter, the imports and the clients come back from the snapshot.

choices.text: Invokes the function on a schedule so one environment stays warm
choices.why: That is the ping, which keeps one environment and no more.

choices.text: Compresses the package so that it downloads faster during init
choices.why: It snapshots an initialised environment; the package is not what it changes.

prompt: create-function with --snap-start ApplyOn=PublishedVersions, against moto 5.2.3, answered ApplyOn: None. What does that show?
hint: What did moto do with the setting?

choices.text: That SnapStart is not available for Python, and the request was turned down
choices.why: AWS documents it for Python 3.12 and later. Nothing was refused: the call succeeded.

choices.text: That moto discarded the setting, which AWS would have kept
choices.why: Right. moto accepted the flag and stored nothing, the quietest failure there is.

choices.text: That SnapStart only takes effect after a version is published
choices.why: That is true of the snapshot, and the setting itself would still read PublishedVersions at once.

choices.text: That SnapStart needs provisioned concurrency on the same version
choices.why: The two do not combine at all.

prompt: Under SnapStart, which of these, made at the top of the file, has to be checked or remade after each restore? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which of them would be wrong if two environments shared it?

choices.text: A random seed
choices.why: Right. Every restored copy would produce the same numbers.

choices.text: A database connection
choices.why: Right. It was opened by an environment that no longer exists.

choices.text: The import of boto3
choices.why: Imported code is the same in every copy, which is the point of the snapshot.

choices.text: A temporary credential
choices.why: Right. It would be shared, and it expires.

choices.text: A configuration file shipped in the package
choices.why: The file is the same everywhere; reading it once is fine.

prompt: A ping invokes a function every five minutes, all day. How many invocations does it add in a 30-day month?
hint: Twelve an hour.

prompt: Put the remedies for a cold start in the order they are worth trying, the cheapest first.
hint: What each one costs, from nothing to every second.
items: Make the module light: fewer imports, a small package
Give the function the memory its init needs
Publish versions and turn on SnapStart
Provisioned concurrency for the hours it matters
trap: Provisioned concurrency comes last because it is billed for every second it is configured, busy or idle.

prompt: A ping keeps one environment warm. Six requests arrive in the same second. How many of them meet a cold start?
hint: One environment serves one request at a time.

prompt: A queue consumer processes a nightly batch and has a cold start of 2 s. What should the team do about it first?
hint: Who waits on the first message?

choices.text: Provisioned concurrency for the hours the batch runs
choices.why: That pays every second to remove a delay nobody sees.

choices.text: A ping every five minutes, all day
choices.why: It adds 288 invocations a day and keeps one environment warm, for a delay nobody notices.

choices.text: Little: nobody waits, so a light module is all it needs
choices.why: Right. A cold start matters in proportion to the person waiting on it, and here nobody is.

choices.text: Turn on SnapStart, because any cold start is a defect to remove
choices.why: A cold start is a cost, and this one costs nobody anything they notice.
